chapterTitle: Why Games Feel So Hard to Stop

summary.coreClaim: Games are sticky for two reasons that compound: they pay strokes (the basic unit of social acknowledgment; negative beats zero) and they confirm life positions (basic I'm OK / not OK stances formed early). Leaving requires replacing the stroke supply first, then updating the position. Without that sequence, stopping produces deprivation, not freedom.
anchorsUsed: Maya and the monthly angry GitHub issue (work)
Inez and Coach Banerjee, the late-night call loop (personal)
Theo's Sunday parenting criticism at Ren's house (personal)
summary.hardDepthTension: Order of operations: replacement first, update second. A player attempting to update their life position in a stroke vacuum returns to the old game. The supply plan is the actual work.
summary.bridgeToNextChapter: With strokes and life positions as the reader's vocabulary, every game in the catalog is asking the same two questions: what is the payoff made of, and which position is it confirming?

strongestQualities: The negative-stroke-as-load-bearing argument is delivered mechanically, not morally: 'Maya's monthly angry issue is doing the work of a positive stroke she does not have a reliable source for. It is the wrong shape and it pays out anyway.'
The order-of-operations limit in P6 is the most practically useful piece of writing in the chapter: it converts 'stop playing' from a platitude into a diagnostic problem.

The Theo/Ren anchor carries the life position concept through a sustained concrete example (two years of Sunday visits, retirement, necessity) that makes the position visible as an organizing structure, not just a mood.
